newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin moves to rest home, meets chief-of-staff.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin moves to rest home, meets chief-of-staff.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, continuing his steady convalescence after heart surgery, left hospital on Friday for a government rest home where he held talks with Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais.

Chief Kremlin doctor Sergei Mironov told a news conference the president would spend two or three weeks at the Barvikha sanatorium just outside Moscow, where he would gradually step up his workload and physical activity.
Yeltsin's convalescence from quintuple heart bypass surgery on November 5 was going to plan and was scheduled to be complete around December 20, Mironov said.
The president could even make some trips before then to the Kremlin, where his long absence triggered jostling for influence among his entourage and put many of Russia's problems on hold.
Yeltsin was already working four to six hours a day and had meetings scheduled for almost every day he will be at Barvikha.

NTV commercial television showed Yeltsin, wearing a fur hat and long dark coat, waving cheerfully as he stepped into the presidential Mercedes-Benz limousine for the short drive from the Central Clinical Hospital to Barvikha.
Kremlin press spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news conference that Yeltsin was feeling well and that he met Chubais at midday (0900 GMT) at the sanatorium.
"The president was clearly in a good mood when he left the Central Clinical Hospital," Yastrzhembsky said.
Yeltsin, 65, has been making steady progress but doctors have warned him against taking things too fast.
Mironov said there was no question of the president "forcing" the pace of his recovery.
Yastrzhembsky said doctors were satisfied with his progress.
"The president's blood pressure is normal and his pulse averages 80," he said, quoting doctors who examined Yeltsin just before he left the hospital.

On Wednesday, in his first public appearance since before his operation, Yeltsin said he was in fighting mood and would return to work after a spell in Barvikha. Mironov warned, however, that he should not overdo things.
Yeltsin was shown walking slowly and stiffly with his wife, daughter and granddaughter in the hospital grounds but he spoke in a firm voice and there was colour in his cheeks.
Mironov said that during his time at Barvikha, Yeltsin would start extending the distances he walked, undertake physiotherapy exercises and massages.

At the end of the convalescence around Decmeber 20, the president would be fully fit for the strains of office, although as with any heart patient cardiologists would keep him under observation for a time.
He could have another 10 to 12 years of full working life, the doctor said, and live for much longer.

Asked about reports that Yeltsin had been indulging his passion for the "banya", the sauna-like Russian steam bath, Mironov said the president had indeed had two or three minutes of light steaming. But he had not gone for the full treatment, which involves long periods of hot steam followed by cold baths.

In a month or so, Yeltsin would be allowed to make longer journeys, including crossing time zones, Mironov said. He denied that the presidential jet had been equipped with an intensive care system but said it did have some medical facilities.
